summary: A status update from BBN on the troubled release of IMPSYS 2600. It recaps the attempts on May 15, May 31 and June 6, where the TIP version failed badly and the old systems were put back. It reports on later efforts to get the new system running.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 359 reports that attempts to switch the ARPANET to IMP system 2600 had repeatedly been rolled back. It summarizes the problems encountered and gives planned dates for trying again.

subtitle: A June 1972 update on repeated attempts to bring the new IMP system online.

tldr.problem: The new IMP system, release 2600, could not yet remain running across the network because distribution, system, and TIP problems disrupted rollout attempts.
tldr.mechanism: The report recounts the trial dates, their outcomes, and the next planned attempts.
tldr.outcome: As of June 22, 1972, the new system was not up. RFC 359 obsoletes RFC 343.

today: RFC 359 is listed with status Unknown and obsoletes RFC 343. It is a status report describing the situation on June 22, 1972.

sections.title: The System Was Still Not Up
sections.content:
Dave Walden reports on the attempted release of the new IMP system, release 2600. His opening statement is that the system had still not been brought up successfully.

The report obsoletes RFC 343 and recounts the rollout attempts through June 21, 1972.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system had not yet stayed in operation. The report explains what happened during the attempts so far.

sections.title: Four Rollout Attempts
sections.content:
The first attempt, on May 15, underestimated the difficulty of distributing the system to more than twenty-five sites and did not reach debugging. On May 31, the team debugged it but found problems that prevented leaving it up.

On June 6, the IMP system worked fairly well but the matching TIP system did not, so the old systems were restored. The June 20 attempt left the new systems up, but TIP crashes reached about one per hour by the afternoon of June 21, prompting another rollback.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attempt exposed a different obstacle: distribution, system problems, TIP compatibility, and repeated TIP crashes. The operators restored the old systems after the problems appeared.

sections.title: The Next Planned Tests
sections.content:
The authors planned to skip June 27 and July 4, then try again Thursday, July 6, 1972. If needed, another attempt was planned for Tuesday, July 18, and following Tuesdays, under the schedule in RFC 343.

The report notes that one TIP crash per hour across the network meant about one crash every eight or ten hours when debugging with one TIP.
sections.plainLanguage: The next attempt was planned for July 6, with later attempts if needed. Because crashes were spread across the network, a single TIP could take hours to fail during debugging.

references.text: RFC 343, referenced for the schedule of subsequent release attempts.
